title: Caching is the Unglamorous Lever for Affordable LLM Scale
linkedin_md:
# Caching is the Unglamorous Lever for Affordable LLM Scale

Building production LLM systems means facing the bill. Token costs are the dominant operational expense. When your system scales, those costs scale linearly with usage unless you intervene. Caching is that intervention. It’s not a new AI model or a fancy framework. It’s a fundamental engineering lever that turns cost curves from linear to sub-linear.

The math is simple but forceful. A single complex prompt to a top-tier model can cost a few cents. At ten thousand queries per hour, that’s hundreds of dollars per hour. Most production workloads have significant redundancy. Users ask similar questions. Batch jobs process similar data. Without caching, you pay the LLM provider to compute the same answer, repeatedly.

## The Two Layers of Cache

Effective caching for LLMs operates at two levels: the prompt level and the embedding level.

Prompt-level caching is straightforward. You hash the exact input prompt and model parameters. On a cache hit, you return the stored completion. This is highly effective for deterministic, repetitive queries. The hit rate dictates savings. A 40% hit rate on a high-volume endpoint can cut costs by nearly half. The tradeoff is granularity. A single changed word creates a new cache key, a new miss. This works best for backend workflows, API calls from other services, and repeated user actions.

Embedding-level caching, or semantic caching, is for variable natural language. Here, you cache based on the semantic meaning of the input, not its exact string. You generate an embedding vector for the new query. If its distance to a cached query’s embedding is below a threshold, you return the cached completion. This handles paraphrases and similar intents. The tradeoffs are nuanced: the cosine similarity threshold, embedding model choice, and vector search latency. A looser threshold increases hit rates but risks returning inaccurate, contextually wrong answers.

## Implementing the Cache

The implementation is more important than the concept. A naive Redis setup can get you started, but scaling requires design.

First, decide on invalidation. Time-based expiration (TTL) is simplest. It works for non-evolving data. Content-based invalidation is harder. If the underlying knowledge source updates, you must purge related cache entries. This often requires tagging entries with metadata, like document IDs, and building a purge pipeline.

Second, monitor like it’s a core service. Track the cache hit rate, cost savings, and latency impact. Most importantly, track the error rate or quality metrics on cache hits. A semantic cache returning a slightly off answer can silently degrade user experience. Implement shadow mode for new cache layers: log what *would* have been returned from the cache while still calling the LLM, and compare.

Third, structure your code for fallback. The cache must be a resilient acceleration layer, not a critical path. Circuit breakers should exist. If the vector database is slow, the system should bypass semantic caching and proceed to the LLM call, perhaps with prompt-level caching still in play.

[YOUR STORY HERE - 2-3 paragraphs]

## The Pragmatic Tradeoff

Caching introduces state and complexity to a potentially stateless system. It’s a classic tradeoff: spend engineering cycles to reduce operational spend. The breakeven point comes quickly at scale. If your monthly LLM spend is in the thousands of dollars, a few weeks of engineering effort to build a robust caching layer pays for itself in months.

Start with prompt-level caching on your most expensive, repetitive endpoints. The ROI is almost immediate. Move to semantic caching only when you have quantified the redundancy in natural language queries and can tolerate the semantic similarity risk. Use open-source embedding models for the cache lookup; you don’t need GPT-4 to judge similarity for caching.

This isn’t about hype. It’s about arithmetic. Building affordably at scale means pulling every unglamorous lever you have. Caching is one of the biggest.
